common_name: Archer's Gold Thyme (Golden Creeping Groundcover Thyme)

planting.note: Root cuttings or plant divisions in spring in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Archer's Gold produces bright golden-yellow foliage year-round, most vivid in full sun, over a low, spreading, groundcover habit.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Archer's Gold is a low, spreading thyme selection valued as much for its bright, glowing golden-yellow foliage, which holds its color through the growing season, as for its mild, lemon-tinged thyme flavor and fragrance. It forms a dense, low mat well suited to edging a path, filling gaps between paving stones, or spilling over a rock garden wall, and small lavender-pink flowers appear in summer, drawing bees. Like other thymes it needs sharp drainage and full sun to thrive, quickly declining in heavy, wet soil, and a light shearing after flowering keeps the mat dense and encourages fresh new growth.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Irene is a vigorous, low, trailing rosemary well suited to cascading over a wall, raised bed edge, or large container.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Irene is a vigorous, low-growing, trailing rosemary selection that spreads and cascades rather than growing upright, making it an excellent choice for spilling over a retaining wall, raised bed, or large container edge. It carries the same fragrant, needle-like foliage and culinary use as upright rosemary types, along with small blue flowers in spring, and it tolerates heat and drought exceptionally well once established. Good drainage is essential, since rosemary quickly develops root rot in heavy, wet soil, and only minimal pruning is needed to keep the trailing habit tidy.

common_name: Huntington Carpet Rosemary (Extremely Prostrate Groundcover Rosemary)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Huntington Carpet is one of the most prostrate rosemary selections available, hugging the ground closely and spreading widely, making it a strong choice as a large-scale groundcover on a sunny slope.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Huntington Carpet is among the most flat-growing, ground-hugging rosemary cultivars available, spreading widely while staying only a few inches tall, making it an excellent choice for covering a sunny bank or slope, cascading over a wall, or filling a large container where a true groundcover habit is wanted rather than an upright shrub form. It shares the same fragrant, culinary-quality foliage as other rosemary cultivars and produces small blue flowers in season. Excellent drainage is essential, since rosemary is highly prone to root rot in heavy or poorly drained soil, and it needs very little pruning to maintain its naturally flat, spreading form.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Severn Sea has an arching, semi-trailing habit intermediate between fully upright and fully prostrate rosemary types, with deep blue flowers that are showier than many rosemary cultivars.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Severn Sea is a compact, semi-trailing rosemary cultivar with gracefully arching branches, striking a middle ground between the tall, upright habit of culinary types like Tuscan Blue and the fully flat, prostrate groundcover forms. It produces an especially heavy show of deep violet-blue flowers in spring, showier than many other rosemary cultivars, in addition to fragrant, flavorful foliage suitable for cooking. It performs well in a container, raised bed, or rock garden where its arching form can spill attractively over an edge, and like all rosemary it needs sharp drainage and full sun to thrive.

planting.note: Set out only after nights stay reliably above 50 degrees F in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; West Indian lemongrass is the classic culinary type used in Southeast Asian and Caribbean cooking, forming a large, dense clump of aromatic, citrus-scented leaves.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun once nights stay warm. West Indian lemongrass is the standard culinary lemongrass of Southeast Asian and Caribbean cooking, forming a large, dense, fountain-like clump of long, narrow, intensely citrus-scented leaves surrounding thickened, tender stalk bases that are harvested, crushed, and used to flavor soups, curries, teas, and marinades. Unlike East Indian lemongrass, which is grown mainly for essential oil production and has a somewhat harsher aroma, West Indian lemongrass has the milder, sweeter citrus fragrance preferred for cooking. In zone 9 the clump usually dies back after a hard freeze but often regrows from the roots in spring if mulched heavily; in colder zones it is best grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter or replanted annually.
